subject: Cooking
title: Indian Roti and Chapati: Unleavened Simplicity
description: A 60-second lesson on Indian Roti and Chapati: Unleavened Simplicity.

hook.text: A billion people eat roti or chapati daily. Two ingredients. No oven. No yeast. Pure simplicity.

buildup.text: Whole wheat flour (atta) and water are kneaded into soft dough and cooked on a flat tawa griddle.

discovery.text: Steam trapped inside puffs the roti like a balloon — the 'phulka' technique requires exact heat and timing.

twist.text: Roti's simplicity hides complexity — the grind of the flour, water ratio, and resting time all matter critically.

climax.text: In Indian households, the quality of roti is traditionally a measure of a cook's fundamental skill.

punchline.text: The simplest bread demands the most skill.

quiz.question: What makes roti puff up like a balloon during cooking?

details.summary: Roti and chapati are unleavened whole wheat flatbreads cooked on a tawa griddle, eaten daily by hundreds of millions across South Asia. Made from just atta flour and water, they puff from internal steam when exposed to direct flame.
details.whyItMatters: Roti demonstrates that bread at its most elemental — flour, water, and heat — feeds more people daily than any artisan loaf. It is a reminder that bread need not be complex to be essential.
takeaways: Made from only whole wheat atta flour and water
Puffs on direct flame as internal steam separates layers
Eaten daily by hundreds of millions across South Asia

faq.question: What is the difference between roti and chapati?
faq.answer: The terms are often used interchangeably. Technically, chapati is cooked only on a tawa griddle while roti can also be puffed over direct flame. Regional usage varies — in some areas roti is the general term for any flatbread, while chapati specifically means the thin, whole wheat version.

faq.question: Why does roti puff up over a flame?
faq.answer: When roti moves from the griddle to direct flame, intense bottom heat rapidly converts trapped moisture to steam. The cooked surface layers are sealed enough to trap this steam, inflating the bread like a balloon. Proper dough hydration and even rolling are essential for full puffing.
